section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia

text: Abstract
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Abstract

text: Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling. The synergistic efects between TW and other additives were verified by means of chronopotentiometry, cyclic voltammetry, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The outcomes of the electrochemical tests revealed that the competitive adsorption behavior between bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and TW is contingent upon the current density and the intensity of convection. Metallographic section analysis demonstrated that TW exhibits outstanding microvia filling capabilities for micro blind vias with a diameter of 150 µm and a depth of 80 µm. Notably, TW-80 was able to attain a filling rate of 96.15% following electrodeposition for 60 min at a current density of 2 A/dm2. Quantum chemical calculations suggested that the relatively smaller band gap and the clustered molecular structure of TW-80 are more conducive to its adsorption onto the electrode surface, leading to the formation of a barrier layer, which in turn restrains the deposition of copper.

text: Introduction
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction

text: In the realm of microelectronics manufacturing, acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has emerged as a pivotal process, ensuring reliable electrical interconnections within printed circuit boards (PCBs) and advanced packaging substrates [1–4]. The quality of via filling, characterized by void—free and uniform deposition, directly impacts the performance, reliability, and miniaturization potential of electronic devices [5–7]. To achieve this, a complex mixture of additives, including suppressors, accelerators, and levelers, is incorporated into the electroplating bath [8–11]. Among these, suppressors play a crucial role in controlling the deposition rate at diferent surface sites, preventing over—plating at the via openings and promoting bottom—up filling.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction

text: The additives utilized in the acidic sulfate copper plating process primarily consist of chloride ions (Cl-) [12], accelerators, suppressors and levelers. These additives interact with one another to enhance the performance of resulting formed copper plating layer [13, 14, 5, 15–17]. Previous research on suppressors for acid copper electroplating has predominantly focused on polymers and surfactants with diverse molecular structures. For instance, polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based polymers have been widely studied and utilized as suppressors due to their ability to adsorb on the copper surface and inhibit the deposition reaction [18, 19]. However, their high molecular weight and complex synthesis processes often lead to issues such as poor bath stability and dificulty in waste treatment, raising environmental concerns. Polyetheramine (PEP) has also been investigated as a potential suppressor, leveraging its unique amine-containing structure that allows for specific interactions with the copper surface [17, 20]. While PEP shows promise in adjusting the deposition rate, its relatively high cost and limited biodegradability pose challenges for large—scale industrial application.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction

text: Additionally, ethylene—propylene copolymer (EPE) has been explored, as its alternating structure can provide a balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties, influencing the deposition behavior [21, 22]. Nevertheless, EPE may sufer from inconsistent performance under varying electroplating conditions, and its efect on the quality of microvia filling in high—aspect—ratio scenarios remains suboptimal. Moreover, some non—ionic surfactants like Triton X—series have been investigated, but they may exhibit limited eficiency in microvia filling under high— aspect—ratio conditions and can also pose potential toxicity risks.

text: Tween compounds, a class of non—ionic surfactants derived from sorbitan esters and ethylene oxide, have found extensive applications across multiple industries. In the pharmaceutical industry, Tween compounds are commonly used as solubilizers and emulsifiers in drug formulations. They enhance the solubility of poorly water—soluble drugs, improving drug delivery and bioavailability. For example, in the formulation of oral suspensions and injectable emulsions, Tween 80 efectively stabilizes the dispersed phases, ensuring uniform drug distribution [23]. In the food industry, Tween compounds serve as emulsifiers, preventing the separation of oil and water phases in products such as margarine, salad dressings, and ice creams. They also contribute to the texture and shelf—life of food products [24]. In the cosmetics industry, Tween compounds are utilized in creams, lotions, and shampoos for their excellent wetting and emulsifying properties, facilitating the dispersion of ingredients and enhancing product stability [25].

text: Against this backdrop, considering their excellent emulsifying, dispersing, and wetting properties, as well as their relatively low toxicity and good biodegradability, Tween compounds present a compelling option for electroplating applications. However, their application as suppressors in acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has remained largely unexplored. This study aims to investigate the inhibitory efects of TW-20 and TW-80 (as shown in Fig. 1) and their synergistic efects with other additives through electrochemical methods, optical microscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. By doing so, it systematically evaluates Tween compounds as eco-friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, filling this research gap. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the development of more environmentally friendly and eficient electroplating processes, meeting the growing demands of the microelectronics industry for sustainable manufacturing.

text: The electrochemical measurements were performed with a CHI760E (ChenHua) electrochemical workstation, which was furnished with the conventional three electrodes and a 100 mL three-electrode cell capable of accommodating an virgin makeup solution (VMS) of 220 g/L CuSO4·5H2O and 28.33 mL/L H2SO4. A platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) with a diameter of 5 mm was employed as the working electrode, while a copper strip with a diameter of 4 mm served as the counter electrode. The experiment utilized a mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE) as the reference electrode. To evaluate the electroplating efects of the additives, the deposition potential at various rotating disk speeds was measured using chronopotentiometry. A pre-plating step was performed to deposit a 500 nm layer of copper on the platinum spinning disk electrode prior to conducting the chronopotentiometry test. The temperature of the electrolyte was maintained at a constant value of 293 ±1K throughout the duration of the experiment. Chronopotentiometry were conducted using diferent current density at 100 rpm and 1000 rpm respectively. The potential diference measured by the chronopotentiometry was defined as Eq. (1).

text: The PCB test panels had a thickness of 1 mm, with a via diameter ranging from 120 to 150 µm and a via depth of 75 µm. Electroplating processes were conducted in a haring cell with a capacity of 1.5 L and the electroplating solution maintained a flow rate of 2.0 L per minute. The area of the cathode test plate immersed in the electroplating solution measures 50 mm × 60 mm, while the total area of the test plate is approximately 80 mm × 60 mm. In order to enhance the electrical conductivity between the copper plating and the Cu seed layer, the test boards underwent a series of decontamination processes before plating. The specific operational procedure is as follows: acid cleaning agent followed by deionized water rinse, micro-etching, another deionized water rinse, acid dipping, and finally copper electroplating in an acid bath. The electroplating test was conducted at ambient temperature with the current density maintained at 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 A/dm2 for various plating durations. Continuous agitation was achieved by stirring the solution with flowing air bubbles to ensure thorough mixing of the plating solution and facilitate efective mass transfer in the plating cell.

text: Calculation Methods
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Calculation Methods

text: The molecular structures of TW-20 and TW-80 were optimized using the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) method with Gaussian09 W software. The optimization of Tween's molecular structure was conducted based on frontier molecular orbital theory, focusing on the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) [29]. The forcite module and VMD software were respectively adopted to investigate the interaction between copper surface and Tween and visualize the optimized geometry and molecular orbitals [30]. Tween molecular dynamics properties in the aqueous phase such as radius of gyration, radial distribution function and diffusion coeficient were investigated by the Material Studio software at the temperature of 298 K. The COMPASSII force field was utilized to optimize the size and simulate the adsorption process of Tween.

text: In general, a lower Q value signifies a more potent inhibitory efect of the inhibitor. These outcomes suggest that as the concentration of inhibitors increase, both TW-20 and TW-80 reach their maximum inhibitory strength at a concentration of 100–200 mg/L. Additionally, within the concentration range of 50–200 mg/L, TW-80 demonstrates a superior inhibitory efect compared to TW-20. The findings of this experiment align with previous research [31], which demonstrates that inhibitors with larger molecular weights exhibit stronger inhibitory capabilities when their molecular structures are consistent.

text: Following the determination of the inhibitory strengths of the two inhibitors, this study utilized the chronopotentiometry to predict the hole-filling capacity of the plating solution consisting of 60 mg/L Cl-, 6 mg/L accelerator, 4 mg/L HPTT and separate batches of 200 mg/L TW-20 or TW-80. The test results are shown in Fig. 4. The analysis of the test results indicated that the plating solutions containing distinct inhibitors all adhered to the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of additives [32], as evidenced by a notable negative shift in the stable potential measured at high rotation speeds. In other words, the inhibitors exhibit a stronger inhibitory efect under conditions of strong convection, thereby complicating the process of copper deposition. Furthermore, it can be inferred from Fig. 4 that the overpotential for copper deposition with TW-80 is higher than that with TW-20, which remains unafected by the intensity of convection. After comparing the potential diference Δη calculated for the two inhibitors at diferent rotation speeds, it becomes apparent that Δη for TW-80 consistently exceeds that for TW-20 at equivalent concentrations.

text: into the plating tank. Subsequently, a test board containing blind holes with diameters ranging from 120–150 μm was immersed in the plating solution. The plating experiments were carried out using deposition current densities of 0.5 A/dm2, 1 A/dm2, and 2 A/dm2. After the metallographic sample was filled with resin, it was polished and subsequently examined and analyzed using a metallographic microscope. Cross-sectional images were obtained to demonstrate the filled blind holes under diferent inhibitors. Figure 5(a-f) show that an increase in current density led to a gradual decrease in the surface copper thickness for both sets of metallographic samples, while the filling rate gradually improved. This phenomenon can be attributed to the higher likelihood of the accelerator replacing the inhibitor at lower current densities, which prolongs the time required for each additive to reach adsorption equilibrium. Consequently, there is minimal diference in the rates of copper deposition between the interior and exterior of the holes over a prolonged period, which leads to a decrease in the filling rate and an increase in the thickness of the surface copper.

text: To further clarify the interaction of these additives, the synergistic efects of TW with other additives were further investigated through chronopotentiometry, as shown in Fig. 6(a-f). The analysis will be based on TW-80 since the structural similarity between TW-20 and TW-80. As illustrated in Fig. 6(b), the leveling agent HPTT does not influence copper deposition under either strong or weak convection intensities. Following the addition of TW, a slight negative shift in the deposition potential is observed. The subsequent introduction of SPS leads to a positive shift in the deposition potential. Finally, the addition of Cl- results in a rapid negative shift in the copper deposition overpotential and an increase in Δη to 20 mV, indicating the occurrence of convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior.

text: Comparing the time intervals of 500–1000 s in Fig. 6(b) with the 1000–1500 s interval in Fig. 6(d) reveals that the simultaneous presence of HPTT and Cl- can accelerate the reduction of copper ions, whereas no such efect is observed when HPTT is present alone. Furthermore, a comparison between the intervals of 500–1500 s in Fig. 6(b) and 500–1000 s in Fig. 6(f) indicates that when only HPTT and TW are present in the VMS, HPTT diminishes the inhibitory efect of TW, suggesting an antagonistic interaction between the two. This antagonism reduces the adsorption capacity of both HPTT and TW in regions of strong convection, while exhibiting no significant impact under weak convection conditions. This implies that HPTT accelerates the rate of copper deposition outside blind holes, leading to an increase in the thickness of the deposited copper.

text: Moreover, when analyzing the time intervals of 500–2000 s in Fig. 6(d) alongside those of 500–1500 s in Fig. 6(f), it becomes evident that the addition of Cl- disrupts the antagonistic interaction between TW and HPTT. TW and Cl- preferentially combine to form a TW-Cl- complex, significantly enhancing the inhibitory efect on copper deposition. This suggests that in the simultaneous presence of Cl-, HPTT, and TW, Cl- preferentially associates with TW, thereby augmenting its inhibitory efect.

text: Following the determination of the optimal concentrations of TW-20 and TW-80, they were subsequently fixed at 100 mg/L. The relationship between their inhibitory strength and Cl- concentration was then investigated using CV to ascertain the corresponding optimal Cl- concentration, as illustrated in Fig. 7(a-b). As the concentration of Cl- in the electrolyte rises, there is an initial increase followed by a decrease in the cathodic polarization of copper ion deposition, which aligns with the pattern of initially decreasing and then increasing copper dissolution peaks. Moreover, with the gradual increase in Cl- concentration, the current–potential"hysteresis loop"resulting from distinct scan directions is notably attenuated [33]. Figure 7(a) illustrated that at a Cl- concentration of 40 mg/L, TW-20 demonstrates the most pronounced inhibitory impact on copper ion deposition, whereas at a Cl- concentration of 30 mg/L, TW-80 displays the most potent inhibitory efect on copper ion deposition.

text: Continuing to elevate the Cl- concentration not only fails to enhance the inhibitory efect of the surfactants but also accelerates copper deposition, a phenomenon associated with the depolarizing efect of Cl-. The conclusions drawn from the figure are consistent with existing literature [34], suggesting that there is an optimal Cl- concentration for a fixed inhibitor concentration that maximizes its inhibitory efect.

text: The inhibitory potency of TW at the optimal concentration of Cl- was examined through linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), as shown in Fig. 8. The figure clearly demonstrates that the cathodic polarization of copper ion deposition exhibits a gradual increase upon the addition of 100 mg/L of TW to the VMS solution. Nevertheless, the extent of this augmentation in polarization is currently minimal. The observation suggests that elevating the concentration of TW in the plating solution may partially augment its adsorption on the cathode surface, consequently enhancing its inhibitory efect on copper deposition. At this stage, the adsorption of TW on the cathode surface is primarily attributed to electrostatic and van der Waals forces [35], leading to a comparatively mild inhibitory efect. When Cl- was present in the solution, there was a significant increase in the cathodic polarization of copper ion deposition. This is evidenced by a depolarization efect on the copper ion deposition process. The only plausible explanation for this experimental phenomenon is the synergistic interaction between Cl- and TW.

text: The Nyquist plots derived from the plating solutions containing TW-20, TW-80 and diferent concentrations of Cl- are depicted in Fig. 9, along with their corresponding equivalent circuit diagrams. It is important to note that, in order to provide a more objective reflection of the adsorption of inhibitors in the actual copper plating experiment for blind hole filling, the electrochemical impedance data were measured at a polarization potential of −0.65 V (vs. SMSE). The equivalent circuit diagram shows the diferent components representing resistance and capacitance in a system. Rs represents solution resistance, while CPE1 and R1 represent the capacitive arc in the high-frequency region. CPE1 represents double-layer capacitance, while R1 signifies electrochemical reaction resistance. Similarly, CPE2 and R2 correspond to another capacitive arc, indicating Cu + asd relaxation on the electrode surface [36–38]. The magnitude of R1 can indicate the challenges associated with copper ion deposition, enabling the assessment of Cl- concentration on TW's inhibitory capacity against copper deposition.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Electrochemical Behavior of the Additives

text: Table 2 revealed that when the VMS solution contained 100 ppm of TW-20 and 100 ppm of TW-80, an increase in Cl- concentration to 30 mg/L led to the values of R1 increasing from 5.73 Ω cm2 and 5.51 Ω cm2 to 17.17 Ω cm2 and 16.58 Ω cm2, respectively. This finding suggests that, under specific conditions, an elevation in Cl- concentration can significantly enhance the inhibitory efect of TW-20 and TW-80 on copper deposition. Furthermore, when R1 attains its maximum value for TW-20 and TW-80, the associated Cl- concentration aligns with the concentration recorded in prior experiments. In contrast, the absence of additives in the VMS solution results in a R1 value of 4.004 Ω cm2. The comparison of the rise in R1 resulting from the introduction of TW and Cl- concentrations reveals that an elevation in Cl- concentration can more eficiently amplify the inhibitory efect of TW. This phenomenon is closely associated with the adsorption mechanism of TW on the electrode surface. As previously stated, when plating solutions contain higher concentrations of Cl-, TW interacts with Cl- and subsequently adheres to the cathode surface through chemical bonding.

text: In this instance, TW exhibits high adsorption strength, leading to a potent inhibitory impact on copper deposition. Conversely, the absence of Cl- in the plating solution results in the adsorption of TW molecules on the electrode surface through electrostatic or van der Waals forces, which leads to a less robust adsorption and a diminished inhibitory efect on copper ion deposition.

text: Models comprising 500 water molecules and a copper atomic layer were assembled utilizing Material Studio software. The Forcite Energy module was then employed to compute the adsorption energy of TW-20 and TW-80 molecules on the copper layer in a solution without Cl-, as shown in Table 3. The findings suggest that the adsorption energy of TW-80 molecules is considerably more negative than that of TW-20 molecules. This implies that in the absence of Cl-, the binding energy between TW-80 molecules and the copper layer is significantly higher than that of TW-20 molecules, which promotes the adsorption of TW-80 molecules onto the copper layer.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Quantum Chemical Calculations and Molecular Dynamics Simulation

text: The charges of atoms in TW-20 and TW-80 molecules were calculated using Gaussian09 W and GaussView5.0 software. Furthermore, frontier molecular orbital diagrams and ESP images were generated. Due to limitations in the software's ability to accurately calculate charges for large molecular compounds, the molecular structures of TW were simplified for the purposes of this experiment. The findings are presented in supplementary material as Fig. 2 (a)-(f), Fig. 3 and Table 4 below. According to the theory of molecular frontier orbitals, the HOMO (highest occupied molecular orbital) and LUMO (lowest unoccupied molecular orbital) play a crucial role in the adsorption of organic molecules on metal surfaces [39]. A smaller ELUMO value signifies a greater electron-accepting capability, whereas a larger EHOMO value indicates a stronger electron-donating capacity [40, 41]. A narrower band gap (ΔE =ELUMO-EHOMO) indicates higher molecular activity, which is advantageous for adsorption. The data from Table 4 indicates that the ΔE value for TW-80 is comparatively smaller than that for TW-20, suggesting a higher propensity for TW-80 molecules to adsorb onto the copper surface.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Quantum Chemical Calculations and Molecular Dynamics Simulation

text: The ESP image ofers a direct visualization of favored reaction sites, with the red region indicating low electron density and the blue region indicating high electron density. In general, atoms located in regions of high electron density exhibit a stronger tendency to form bonds with metal surfaces [42, 43]. Figure 2 in the supplementary materials indicates that TW-20 and TW-80 molecules possess a comparable distribution of electron density regions as a result of their structural similarity, with both demonstrating elevated electron density at the oxygen atoms. The sole distinction lies in the higher electron density at the carbon–carbon double bond in TW-80 molecules. The higher electron density suggests that the double bond carbon atoms in TW-80 molecules are more prone to forming a carbocation with hydrogen ions in the acidic plating solution. Subsequently, they are more likely to undergo electrophilic addition with Cl -, resulting in chloride adsorbed the copper surface.

text: Based on the aforementioned research findings and pertinent literature [20, 23], this study puts forward an adsorption model for TW-20 and TW-80, as shown in Fig. 13. In the absence of Cl- in the plating solution, TW molecules predominantly adhere to the electrode surface via electrostatic interactions and van der Waals forces, as illustrated in Fig. 3(a1) and (b1) in the supplementary materials. In this scenario, the intermolecular forces between TW molecules and the electrode surface are relatively weak, resulting in a reduced inhibitory effect of the resulting barrier layer on copper deposition. Upon the addition of Cl- to the plating solution, TW molecules engage with Cu + and Cl- to create complexes (TW-Cu + -Cl-). Consequently, it is not just simple TW molecules, but rather these complexes that adsorb on the electrode surface. The TW-Cu + -Cl- complexes adhere to the electrode surface via chemical bonding, resulting in a more potent inhibitory impact on copper deposition due to the formation of a barrier layer. The carbon–carbon double bond in TW-80 molecules specifically undergoes a reaction with Cl- and subsequently adsorbs onto the electrode surface through Cl-.

text: Conclusions
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Conclusions

text: The study shows that TW-20 and TW-80 have inhibitory efects on copper deposition, making them suitable for use as electroplating inhibitors. TW-80 demonstrated exceptional performance, with a plating solution comprising 220 g/L CuSO4·5H2O, 28.33 mL/L H2SO4, 30 mg/L Cl-, 6 mg/L SPS, 8 mg/L L, and 100 mg/L TW-80 achieving full filling of blind holes with a 150 μm diameter, resulting in a filling rate of 95.6%.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Conclusions

text: Electrochemical measurements have uncovered a convection-dependent synergistic efect between TW and L at low current densities. Moreover, a significant synergistic inhibitory efect was observed between TW and Cl-, suggesting that Cl- amplifies the inhibitory efect of TW on copper deposition. The coexistence of TW, L, and Cl- led to the most potent inhibitory efect.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Conclusions

text: Quantum chemical calculations revealed that TW-20 molecules adopt a linear configuration in aqueous solution, whereas TW-80 molecules tend to form a cluster structure, rendering them more susceptible to adsorption on the electrode surface. This results in the formation of a dense and relatively thick barrier layer. The binding energy between TW-80 molecules and the copper layer exhibited a significantly higher magnitude compared to that of TW-20 molecules, indicating a greater propensity for adsorption onto the copper layer. Moreover, the presence of a carbon–carbon double bond in TW-80 molecules was found to enhance their adsorption on the copper layer. Subsequently, the adsorption models of TW-20 and TW-80 were developed based on the aforementioned experimental results.

text: Based on the research on Tween compounds as eco— friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, several key guidelines are proposed. Firstly, when selecting Tween compounds, factors like their hydrophilic—lipophilic balance, molecular weight, and branching structure should be carefully considered to ensure proper adsorption and inhibitory efects. Secondly, concentration optimization is crucial, as both too low and too high concentrations can negatively impact microvia filling quality, thus requiring systematic studies to find the optimal balance. Thirdly, using Tween compounds in combination with other electroplating additives and understanding their synergistic efects can enhance the overall plating performance, although their compatibility and interaction mechanisms need thorough investigation. Finally, environmental considerations are essential, including minimizing compound loss during bath operation and adopting appropriate biodegradation processes for waste treatment.
section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Conclusions

text: By adhering to these guidelines, Tween compounds can be efectively applied, promoting more sustainable and eficient microelectronics manufacturing, and future research should further explore and optimize their application.
